opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was a real turning point for us. I spent many years working on GANs: image-to-image translation, GauGAN, video-to-video synthesis. I still think GANs are beautiful. The adversarial idea is elegant, and when they work, they're incredibly fast at inference. But over time I became convinced that they have a scalability problem.

With GANs, training is a two-player game, and that game is fragile. As you increase the model size or the data diversity, keeping the generator and discriminator in balance gets harder and harder. You get mode collapse, training instability, and a lot of tricks and careful tuning. For a narrow domain like faces, or a dataset with a clear structure, you can make it work very well. But when you want one model to cover the whole visual world, with arbitrary text prompts and huge internet-scale data, every time you scale up you're fighting the optimization rather than benefiting from it.

Diffusion models changed that picture. The training objective is essentially a regression problem, denoising. It's stable, it's well-behaved, and the loss actually tells you something meaningful. When you add more compute, more data, and bigger networks, the results reliably get better. That's the property you want if you believe, as I do, that a lot of progress in AI comes from scaling. So the question I kept asking was not "which model gives the best result on this benchmark today," but "which model will keep improving if we give it ten times or a hundred times more resources?" For GANs I didn't have a confident answer. For diffusion, the evidence was increasingly clear.

So we made the decision to move the team. Honestly, it wasn't easy. We had a lot of expertise and a lot of identity built around GANs, and there's a natural reluctance to walk away from something you're known for. But as a research leader, I feel my job is to put the team where the future is going, not where we've been. We started working on text-to-image diffusion, which led to things like eDiff-I, and later that foundation carried into our work on video and world models.

And I'd add one thing: the lessons from GANs didn't disappear. Ideas like adversarial losses still show up, for example in distillation to make diffusion sampling faster. So it wasn't really abandoning GANs. It was recognizing which framework should be the backbone for scaling, and then bringing the useful pieces along with us.

r001.rationale: Liu says GANs have a scalability problem and that scaling them makes optimization harder, leading him to conclude diffusion was the better framework for future progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So I spent many years on GANs. At NVIDIA we did pix2pixHD, SPADE, GauGAN, StyleGAN came out of the group next door. GANs were very good at what they did. Fast sampling, sharp images, and for a while they were the best thing we had for conditional image synthesis.

But I kept running into the same wall. Every time we wanted to go bigger, more data, more diverse data, a bigger model, the training became fragile. You have this adversarial game between a generator and a discriminator, and the equilibrium is just not stable. You get mode collapse, you get training that diverges after a week, and you spend an enormous amount of engineering effort on tricks: regularization, careful learning rate schedules, architectural hacks. We could make a GAN work beautifully on faces, or on street scenes, because those are narrow distributions. But when we tried to go toward open-domain, internet-scale data, the discriminator just could not keep up, and the generator would cover a small part of the distribution very well and ignore the rest.

So I had this growing feeling that GANs were not a scaling law kind of method. The thing that was happening in language models at that time, where you add more data and more compute and the model just gets better in a predictable way, I did not see that behavior in GANs. More compute often meant more instability, not more capability.

When score-based models and DDPM came out, what struck me was not the sample quality at first, the early results were actually worse than GANs. What struck me was the training objective. It is a simple regression loss. You predict noise, you minimize mean squared error. There is no game, no equilibrium to chase. That means you can scale data, you can scale parameters, and the loss just keeps going down. It behaves like a normal supervised learning problem. And it covers the whole distribution because you are doing likelihood-style training, not trying to fool a critic.

So the decision was really a bet on scalability over short-term quality. I told the team, the sampling is slow now, and the images look worse now, but these are engineering problems, and I believe they will get solved. The instability of GANs is a structural problem, and I do not think it gets solved. That is the kind of trade I am willing to make.

We moved the research team over, and within a year or so we had eDiff-I, and the quality crossed over. And then of course the sampling speed got addressed through distillation, better solvers, consistency models and so on. Looking back, the thing I got right was not any particular technique, it was recognizing which problems are temporary and which ones are fundamental.

r001.rationale: The candidate says GANs were not a “scaling law kind of method,” describes their instability and poor coverage on open-domain, internet-scale data, and calls that instability a structural problem. This clearly communicates that GANs’ lack of scalability would limit their long-term prospects.

astra-6.text:
My concern with GANs was how reliably they would improve as we scaled them. You’re training a generator and a discriminator together, and that balance can be difficult to maintain. A larger model or more compute doesn’t automatically translate into better coverage of the data or better results.

Diffusion offered a more straightforward learning problem: train a model to remove noise. That made it a promising direction for scaling capacity and training, with less of the adversarial balancing act. The tradeoff was slower sampling, but I felt that was worth exploring if it gave us a more dependable path to improving quality and diversity.

So the decision wasn’t that GANs had no future. It was about where we saw the stronger path for continued progress, and that pushed us toward diffusion.

r001.rationale: The response says GANs may not reliably improve with greater scale or compute, then identifies diffusion as a stronger path for continued progress. This communicates that GANs’ scalability concerns could limit their long-term prospects, while clarifying that Liu did not consider GANs to have no future.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the key question was how reliably we could turn more compute and more data into better results. GANs could produce beautiful images, but scaling them was difficult because you were balancing a generator and a discriminator. More capacity didn’t necessarily translate into a predictable improvement.

Diffusion looked like a more straightforward path. You had a denoising objective, and you could focus on scaling the model without managing that adversarial balance. Sampling was slower, so there was a real tradeoff, but I felt that was a problem we could work on. That shifted my thinking toward diffusion as the more promising direction for the team.

r001.rationale: The response says GANs were difficult to scale and that added capacity did not yield predictable improvement, motivating a shift toward diffusion. It does not clearly state that this lack of scalability would limit GANs’ long-term prospects.
